articles.title: Golden Cases Rot: Schedule a Discriminative-Power Audit
articles.excerpt: A case that can no longer fail is no longer a test. Eval suites grow by addition and almost never shrink, which is why a mature suite can sit at a 0.97 pass rate and still catch nothing you did not al…
articles.body: A case that can no longer fail is no longer a test. Eval suites grow by addition and almost never shrink, which is why a mature suite can sit at a 0.97 pass rate and still catch nothing you did not already know. The audit below gives every golden case a measurable ability to reject wrong answers, then schedules that measurement so rot surfaces in weeks instead of quarters. It needs no paid judge model, which matters for the scoring panel further down. Two failure modes hide behind a green dashboard. Saturation is the gradual one: a case written when the model was weaker still passes, and now every model passes it on every run, so it burns latency and returns no signal.
articles.author: Dakota Ma

articles.title: Smart Constructors in Scala 3: Validate Once, Trust Everywhere
articles.excerpt: Opaque types give you shape safety, but not value safety. Here's how smart constructors and ValidatedNec close the gap. This lesson assumes you have used Either or have a brief exposition to the cats…
articles.body: Opaque types give you shape safety, but not value safety. Here's how smart constructors and ValidatedNec close the gap. This lesson assumes you have used Either or have a brief exposition to the cats library. You've wrapped your primitives in opaque types and modeled your domain with ADTs. Nice. But there's still a hole: if the constructor is public, nothing stops someone from writing Email("lol") or Age(-5) . Types give you shape safety. They don't give you value safety. For that you need smart constructors. What's a smart constructor? It's just a function (usually called parse , of , from or apply ) that is the only way to create a value of a type, and that validates its input on the way in.

articles.body: Ultrawings가 Quest 3로 돌아온 날, 저는 안경을 고쳐 쓰며 '보는 것'의 아키텍처를 다시 생각했습니다 UploadVR 헤드라인에 뜬 Ultrawings 1&2 재출시 소식. 개발자 커뮤니티에서는 패스스루 해상도, 핸드 트래킹 레이턴시, 렌더 파이프라인 최적화 같은 이야기가 오갔습니다. 하지만 제 머릿속엔 다른 질문이 맴돌았습니다. '이 하드웨어로, 누군가의 세상을 입체로 되돌릴 수 있을까?' 1. 문제 공간: 양안 시각, 그리고 브로카 영역이 놓친 신호 약시(amblyopia, 흔히 'lazy eye'라 부릅니다)는 단순히 한 눈이 '나쁜' 게 아닙니다. 뇌가 한쪽 눈의 신호를 억제(suppression)해 버린 상태죠. 기존 치료 — 신체적 패치(occlusion therapy)나 적청 안경(anaglyph) — 은 단안 자극에 의존합니다. 하지만 깊이 인식(depth perception)과 입체시(stereopsis)는 양안 융합(binocular fusion)에서만 나옵니다. 패치로 강한 눈을 가려도, 뇌가 두 눈의 신호를 '동시에' 처리하는 법을 익히지 못하면 3D 세상은 여전히 평면으로 남습니다. 제가 처음 이 문제를 마주한 건 2022년 겨울, 서울 합정동 작은 안과 병원에서였습니다. 다섯 살 난 조카가 패치를 붙이고 울고 있었죠. "이거 얼마나 더 해야 해?" 물으니 의사가 말했습니다. "뇌가 배우게 하는 거예요. 근데 아이가 싫어해서…." 그 말이 머릿속에 남았습니다. 하드웨어는 준비됐는데, 소프트웨어가 아이를 기다려주지 못하는구나. 2.

articles.title: A 200 Response Is Not a Contract: Canary Tests for Third-Party Model Endpoints
articles.excerpt: A provider can rename a field, change what finish_reason means, or quietly swap the model behind your endpoint. Your client keeps getting HTTP 200 the whole time. Logs look green, and a user is starin…
articles.body: A provider can rename a field, change what finish_reason means, or quietly swap the model behind your endpoint. Your client keeps getting HTTP 200 the whole time. Logs look green, and a user is staring at a half-finished sentence with no error attached. This is a testing article, not a model-selection article. It assumes you already picked an endpoint — paid, self-hosted, or free — and asks a narrower question: how do you find out that its behaviour moved before your users do? The answer is a contract test suite plus a nightly canary that runs somewhere that isn't your product's host. Both are small. Both are boring. That is the point. The failure classes worth testing Not everything a provider does is a bug. Some of it is a documented version change that still breaks your call site.

articles.title: Stripe Webhooks in Next.js: Idempotency, Out-of-Order Events, and Retries (2026)
articles.excerpt: By Jake Mcdonald, founder of ShipEmber · November 5, 2026 · About a 10-minute read · Checked against Stripe's webhook docs I'm Jake Mcdonald. Most first Stripe webhook handlers look about the same: ve…
articles.body: By Jake Mcdonald, founder of ShipEmber · November 5, 2026 · About a 10-minute read · Checked against Stripe's webhook docs I'm Jake Mcdonald. Most first Stripe webhook handlers look about the same: verify the signature, flip the user to Pro, return 200. Fifteen lines, and it works fine in test mode. Then you read the "Event delivery behaviors" section of Stripe's docs and notice three assumptions hiding in those fifteen lines that aren't true: that each event arrives once, that events arrive in order, and that if your code fails, nothing bad happens. This post is the version I wish I'd read first.
articles.author: Jake Mcdonald

articles.title: I scanned 163 Terraform repos to find out what a shared module change could affect
articles.excerpt: When you have a few repositories, keeping track of dependencies between them is pretty straightforward. But what happens when you have 50, 100, or even 200 repositories? Imagine you're about to update…
articles.body: When you have a few repositories, keeping track of dependencies between them is pretty straightforward. But what happens when you have 50, 100, or even 200 repositories? Imagine you're about to update a shared Terraform module. Before merging, you want to know: Which repositories are using it? Which versions are they using? Are there other repositories that depend on those repositories? Who might be affected by the change? GitHub search can help, but manually piecing together all those relationships gets tedious pretty quickly. I wanted a way to answer those questions without setting up a service or maintaining a separate dependency catalog. So I built RippleMap , an open-source CLI that automatically maps dependencies across repositories.

articles.title: Have you ever thought of Floating Clipboard?
articles.excerpt: One extra Ctrl+C replaced the thing I still needed. It happened often enough that I built a Windows app to stop it. A client reply. A code snippet. A useful link. A color from a design. Copy one more…
articles.body: One extra Ctrl+C replaced the thing I still needed. It happened often enough that I built a Windows app to stop it. A client reply. A code snippet. A useful link. A color from a design. Copy one more thing, and getting back to the previous item breaks your flow. It sounds small, but repeating that interruption all day quietly drains momentum. Windows already has clipboard history. I wanted something that could stay beside my work, remain searchable, and keep reusable content organized without sending it to the cloud. That frustration became FloatClip: a floating clipboard companion for Windows 10 and 11.

articles.excerpt: NASA's Voyager 1 probe is back in communication after the 49-year-old spacecraft briefly fell silent last month, during its interstellar-space mission.
articles.body: Voyager, 1, humanity's most distant spacecraft, is back in contact after briefly losing touch with Earth last month. The spacecraft stopped phoning home for about 48 hours between Oct. 18 and 20 due to a communications glitch that Voyager 1 resolved on its own, before engineers could send the long-running spacecraft a remote fix. "This is the first time we've seen the spacecraft do something like this, but we are also at a point in the mission where we have to expect the unexpected," Kareem Badaruddin, Voyager mission manager at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), said in an agency statement about the incident on Oct. 29.

articles.title: NASA astronaut Jessica Watkins is the 1st Black woman to command a space mission. Will we see more diversity in the future on the final frontier?
articles.excerpt: "Diversity makes the crew stronger."
articles.body: When Jessica Watkins became commander of her mission to the International Space Station, she didn't just fulfill her duty as an astronaut — she made history. Watkins is commanding SpaceX's Crew-13 mission , which launched her and three other astronauts to the I nternational Space Station on Oct. 1. As their Crew Dragon capsule lifted off atop a Falcon 9 rocket that day, Watkins became the first Black woman to command a crewed mission to space. Spaceflight and space science are historically white and male-dominated fields, so this milestone carries incredible significance. "This is certainly an important milestone, I think both for our agency and for the country," Watkins said in a press briefing ahead of Crew-13's launch. This is Watkins' second spaceflight.
